source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 1 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section C is about how an organization is directed, how it deals with uncertainty and how it keeps its objectives within reach. It covers governance roles and models, culture and ethics, risk types and the risk management cycle, risk appetite and tolerance, control types, and why organizations use risk and control frameworks. Throughout, management owns risks and controls; the internal auditor assesses them and reports. In these notes 'must' marks a requirement of the Standards, and 'should' or 'may' marks a consideration: preferred or optional practice that is not mandatory.
analogy: Think of a cargo ship. The owners' board picks the destination and says how much rough weather it will accept: that is governance and risk appetite. The captain and officers plan the route, watch the forecast and decide when to slow down or change course: risk management. The crew uses checklists, alarms, watertight doors and lifeboats: controls. An independent surveyor walks the ship, tests the alarms and tells the owners and the captain what was found. The surveyor never takes the wheel, because then nobody independent would be left to judge the steering.

topics.overview: Governance is how a board directs and oversees an organization. This topic covers what governance includes, which party does what, and what governance frameworks, principles and models are for. Most exam questions here ask whose job something is.
can_do: Explain what governance is and how it differs from management
Match a governance duty to its owner: the board, senior management, internal audit or another assurance provider
Recognize what a governance framework, set of principles or model is for

subtopics.name: What Governance Is
subtopics.definition: Governance is how a board steers an organization: the structures and processes it sets up to inform, direct, manage and monitor what the organization does.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Risk management and control sit inside governance. If nobody is clearly in charge of direction and oversight, good controls lower down cannot make up for it, so the chief audit executive (CAE) must understand governance before planning.
how_it_works: Governance is wider than daily management and wider than compliance.
It covers how goals are chosen and how big and everyday decisions get made.
It covers who oversees risk management and control, and how an ethical culture is encouraged.
It covers performance management, accountability, structure, how risk and control information travels and how the board, management and assurance providers work together.
The board delegates authority to management, so a limit it set is the board's to change; an executive raising their own limit is a governance gap, even before any loss.
The CAE must understand all of this before building the strategy and plan (Standard 9.1 Understanding Governance, Risk Management, and Control Processes).
subtopics.example: A public water utility in New Zealand has a board that meets twice a year and receives no risk reports. Internal auditor Aroha is on an engagement (one audit assignment) reviewing procurement controls. The controls look sound, but nobody above the procurement manager ever sees exceptions. Aroha raises the oversight gap with the engagement supervisor as a governance matter, not only a procurement one.

review: Compare the board charter with what the minutes show it oversees
Trace one significant risk from a business unit to the board pack
Inspect how authority to decide is assigned and recorded
evidence: Board and committee minutes for the past year
Board charter and schedule of delegated authority
Risk and performance reports actually sent to the board
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the board, with senior management, to define what it oversees, what information it receives and how often.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how the organization is governed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Governance belongs to the board, which directs and oversees; management runs the organization within it. The internal audit function assesses and reports, and never steers. Must: the CAE understands governance before building the plan (Standard 9.1).

exam_traps.trap: Governance is just another word for management.
exam_traps.why: The board sets governance up to direct and oversee. Its structures do include how the organization is managed, but management carries out strategy inside them and is not its own overseer.

exam_traps.trap: A strong board runs daily operations to keep control.
exam_traps.why: The board directs and monitors. Daily operation is delegated to management.

key_terms.definition: The board's structures and processes for informing, directing, managing and monitoring what the organization does.
Watching and questioning how management runs things, without doing management's job.
Having to answer to someone for results: management to the board, the board to stakeholders.

subtopics.name: Who Does What in Governance
subtopics.definition: Governance roles split four ways: the board directs and oversees, senior management runs the organization, the internal audit function gives independent assurance and advice, and other providers add assurance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Governance questions mostly ask whose job it is. Give a duty to the wrong party, such as strategy to internal audit, and the answer is wrong.
how_it_works: The board sets direction, establishes risk appetite, delegates authority to management and oversees how it is used.
Senior management answers to the board. It designs structures and processes, carries out strategy and manages risks and controls.
In The IIA's Three Lines Model (a Statement of Position, not a Standard: 1A8.1), first-line managers own risks and run controls; second-line roles support, monitor and challenge.
The internal audit function gives independent assurance (an objective assessment that raises confidence) and advice (help without management duties), and reports functionally to the board.
External auditors and regulators serve outside stakeholders, with a scope set by law or regulation, and sit outside the three lines.

The chief audit executive (CAE) must coordinate with other assurance providers, even ones internal audit assesses (Standard 9.5). The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement adds: independence is not isolation.

rows.label: Board
cells: Direct and oversee; establish risk appetite
Stakeholders such as owners, members or the public

rows.label: Senior management
cells: Run the organization; own risks and controls
The board

rows.label: Internal audit function
cells: Independent assurance and advice
The board (functional reporting)

rows.label: External auditor
cells: Independent view on financial statements or other required disclosures
Outside stakeholders, under law or regulation

subtopics.example: At an insurer in Kenya, the chief risk officer asks new internal auditor Wanjiru to write the risk appetite statement, and Wanjiru drafts it. The engagement supervisor stops the draft: establishing appetite is for the board, and its author could not assess it objectively. Wanjiru withdraws it and discloses the drafting to the CAE as a possible impairment.

review: Compare each governance duty in the charters with who performs it
Trace how results from each assurance provider reach the board
evidence: Assurance map showing which provider covers each major risk
Charters of the board, its committees and management committees
Reporting-line chart for risk, compliance and internal audit
audit_focus.recommend: Get senior management and the board to write down, for each major risk area, which party steers, which runs it and which checks it.
audit_focus.decides: The board assigns governance roles; senior management assigns management roles

subtopics.isaca_rule: Board directs and oversees; management owns and manages; internal audit assures and advises. An option that hands internal audit a decision, a policy or a risk is wrong.

exam_traps.trap: The external audit already covers controls, so it can replace internal audit.
exam_traps.why: External auditors give outside stakeholders an independent view within a scope set by law or regulation. They are no substitute for internal assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit should set policy where management has left a gap.
exam_traps.why: Setting policy is a management decision. Internal audit reports the gap and may advise.

key_terms.definition: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
Parties besides internal audit that give assurance, such as compliance, risk management, external auditors and regulators.

subtopics.name: Governance Frameworks, Principles and Models
subtopics.definition: A governance framework, set of principles or model is a published reference describing good governance, so an organization can design and judge its own.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Boards and internal auditors need a yardstick. A recognized reference gives shared language and criteria. The exam tests what these references are for, not their contents.
how_it_works: Principles, frameworks and models overlap: each describes good governance in a form an organization can reuse.
The IIA's Three Lines Model is a governance model of roles, not departments: a small organization with simple risks may have no separate second-line team, unless a regulator requires one.
COSO's internal control and enterprise risk management frameworks both begin with board oversight and culture.
The chief audit executive (CAE) should know the leading principles, frameworks and models, see which the organization uses and gauge how mature its governance is (Standard 9.1, considerations).
Laws, regulators and licenses can add binding rules that beat guidance: the 2026 Three Lines statement lets a CAE supervise second-line roles with safeguards, unless such a rule forbids it.
subtopics.example: A nonprofit landlord in Canada tells its regulator it follows a recognized governance model. Planning a governance engagement, internal auditor Mateus asks which reference the board adopted, proposes its expectations as criteria to the engagement supervisor, then tests the board's and committees' practice against them.

review: Inspect the board record that names the governance reference in force
Compare the reference's expectations with committee practice over the year
evidence: Board resolution or policy naming the adopted reference
Gap assessment against the reference, with owners and dates
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the board to confirm which governance reference applies, and management to close the gaps it shows.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides which governance yardstick applies

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize a governance reference by its purpose: shared language and criteria for directing and overseeing. It does not prove effectiveness and binds only through a law, regulator, contract or the organization's own policy. Should: the CAE knows the leading ones (Standard 9.1, considerations).

exam_traps.trap: An organization that has adopted a recognized governance framework has effective governance.
exam_traps.why: Adoption shows intent. Effectiveness shows in how the board and management behave, which the internal auditor assesses against the reference.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit's independent assurance can replace second-line compliance monitoring.
exam_traps.why: Internal audit visits areas at intervals set by risk; second-line roles may watch higher-risk or compliance-heavy areas on an ongoing basis (The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement).

key_terms.definition: A structured reference that sets out the parts of good governance and how they fit together.
The IIA's model of who owns risk, who supports and challenges, and who gives independent assurance.
How developed and consistently applied a process is, from informal to well established.

topics.overview: Culture is how people in an organization really behave and why; the control environment is the standards, processes and structures every other control rests on. This topic also covers what risks and controls mean inside one engagement, and how the way an organization makes decisions shapes its governance, risk management and control.
can_do: Tell culture and the control environment apart from written policy
Identify the risks and controls that belong to one engagement
Spot how a weak decision process undermines governance, risk management and control

subtopics.name: What Culture and the Control Environment Mean
subtopics.definition: Organizational culture is how people choose to act and work together, and what drives those choices; the control environment is the standards, processes and structures that underpin internal control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Where leaders ignore rules or reward results at any price, well-designed procedures get bypassed. Culture problems often sit behind major control failures.
how_it_works: Culture shows in behavior: what people do when a rule is inconvenient, and what happens to those who speak up.
Formal drivers include goals, incentives and consequences; informal drivers include shared values and beliefs.
COSO's internal control framework puts the control environment first, as the base for every other component.
It includes integrity and ethical values, board oversight, clear authority and responsibility, competent people and accountability.
The board and senior management set the tone at the top; managers at each level strengthen or weaken it.
Culture can be audited through behavior: compare what the organization says it expects with what people are seen to do.
subtopics.example: At a logistics firm in Poland, the code of conduct says safety comes first, yet depot teams are rewarded only for on-time departures, and two supervisors who held trucks back for brake checks were moved aside. Senior internal auditor Tomasz, reviewing fleet maintenance, records both facts as control environment weaknesses, with evidence, and does not rate the area on written policy alone.

review: Compare stated values with incentive plans and promotion decisions
Sample reported concerns and trace how each was handled
Interview staff at several levels about pressure to bypass rules
evidence: Speak-up and incident trend data with outcomes
Incentive plan terms and recent payout records
Staff survey results on how leaders behave
audit_focus.recommend: Get senior management to align incentives and consequences with the stated values and report culture indicators to the board.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management owns the culture program; the board holds it to account

subtopics.isaca_rule: Judge the control environment by what leaders do and reward, not by the policy manual alone. A weak tone at the top weakens every control beneath it. Must: the chief audit executive considers how the organization promotes an ethical culture (Standard 9.1).

exam_traps.trap: Strong written policies mean a strong control environment.
exam_traps.why: Written policies are part of the control environment, but they show only intent. It is strong when leaders model and enforce the standards and when rewards and consequences back them.

exam_traps.trap: The control environment is one more control to test, like an approval.
exam_traps.why: It is the base for every other control: weak integrity, oversight or accountability lowers the reliability of all of them at once.

key_terms.definition: How people in an organization actually behave and work together, and what drives that behavior.
The standards, processes and structures that all other controls rest on.
The example about integrity and control set by the board and senior management.

subtopics.name: Risks and Controls at Engagement Level
subtopics.definition: Engagement-level risks could stop the activity under review from meeting its objectives; engagement-level controls are what management, the board or other parties do to manage them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An engagement cannot test everything. The internal auditor has to find the risks that matter to this activity and the controls meant to manage them, then build objectives, scope and tests around those.
how_it_works: Organization-level risks drive the internal audit plan; engagement-level risks are identified afresh for the one activity being reviewed.
The internal auditor must understand the activity, identify the significant risks to its objectives, consider fraud and rank the risks (Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment).
Inputs include the organization's strategy and risk tolerance, the risk assessment behind the plan, and the activity's own processes and criteria.
Each objective is linked to its risks, and each risk to the control meant to manage it, often in a risk and control matrix.
The wider culture feeds in: weak tone, pressure or poor oversight raises the risk in any single process.
Advisory engagements may not need a formal, written risk assessment; it depends on what was agreed.
subtopics.example: Dawit, an internal auditor at a cement producer in Ethiopia, is planning a review of the spare-parts warehouse. The organization-wide risk assessment lists only 'supply chain disruption'. Dawit walks the process with the warehouse manager and identifies risks such as theft of high-value parts and obsolete stock still valued as usable, with the control for each. Dawit ranks them and proposes objectives and scope to the engagement supervisor.

review: Walk the process end to end before listing any risk
Compare the risk and control matrix with the activity's stated objectives
Confirm fraud risks were considered and ranked with the rest
evidence: Risk and control matrix linking objectives, risks and controls
Walk-through notes and process flowcharts
Risk tolerance statement, where the organization has set one
audit_focus.recommend: Ask process owners to keep their own record of key risks and the control that manages each.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or a delegated engagement supervisor approves objectives and scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must (Standard 13.2): understand the activity, identify the significant risks to its objectives and consider fraud. The plan's risk assessment is an input, not a substitute. For advisory work a formal documented assessment may not be needed.

exam_traps.trap: The organization-wide risk assessment already covers this area, so engagement planning can skip risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: The plan-level assessment is broad. Each engagement needs an understanding of this activity and its own significant risks, or an update of an earlier engagement assessment.

key_terms.definition: The area, process, system or unit that an engagement examines.
The planning step that identifies and ranks the risks of the activity being examined.
A working table that lines up objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage them.

subtopics.name: Decision-Making Processes and Their Effect on Control
subtopics.definition: Decision-making processes are the ways an organization decides: who may decide what, on what information, with what challenge, and how the decision is recorded and reviewed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Governance, risk management and control are carried out through decisions. If decisions are rushed, concentrated in one person or made without risk information, formal controls exist on paper but do not shape what happens.
how_it_works: Clear decision rights say who may approve what; unclear ones lead to gaps, duplication and conflicts of interest.
Good decisions use risk information: those deciding see the risks and how they compare with risk appetite.
Challenge matters: decisions that nobody may question bypass second-line review and board oversight.
Incentives steer decisions; rewarding only speed or sales pushes people to cut around controls.
Understanding governance includes considering how the organization makes its strategic and operational decisions (Standard 9.1).
The internal audit function strengthens decision-making and oversight through assurance and advice; it does not make the decisions.
subtopics.example: A resort group in Fiji lets its founder approve all capital projects alone, usually by phone, with no business case on file. Internal auditor Siosaia reviews a hotel refurbishment that finished on time and under budget. The manager says the result proves the process works. Siosaia still reports the approval route as a governance weakness: no cost estimate, no second view, no record. Siosaia discusses options with management.

review: Trace a sample of major decisions to the approved authority limits
Inspect what risk information reached the deciders, and when
Compare decisions taken outside committee with the escalation rules
evidence: Delegation of authority matrix with approval limits
Decision papers and minutes showing options, risks and dissent
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management define decision rights, the information each decision needs and how it is recorded.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management decide how authority is delegated

subtopics.isaca_rule: Look at how a decision was made, not only at its outcome. Unclear authority, missing risk information or no room for challenge is a governance weakness even when the result was fine. Must: the chief audit executive considers how the organization makes decisions (Standard 9.1).

exam_traps.trap: The decision turned out well, so the decision process needs no comment.
exam_traps.why: A good outcome can hide a weak process. The auditor assesses whether authority, information and challenge were in place.

exam_traps.trap: Faster decisions with fewer approvals always mean weaker control.
exam_traps.why: Speed is not the test. What matters is clear authority, the right information and challenge in proportion to the risk.

key_terms.definition: The agreed rules on who may decide or approve what, and up to what limit.
The formal passing of decision power from the board to management and downward, with limits.
A manager using their position to set a control aside.

topics.overview: Organizations must meet laws, regulations, contracts, their own policies and the ethical standards they have set. This topic covers how to recognize each kind of requirement, what the internal auditor does in the ethics framework without owning it, and how a concern is reported.
can_do: Name the source of a requirement: law, regulation, contract, policy or ethical expectation
Separate what the internal auditor does in the ethics framework from what management owns
Choose the right channel and level for reporting an ethics or compliance concern

subtopics.name: Ethical, Legal and Compliance Requirements
subtopics.definition: Ethical, legal and compliance requirements are the rules and expectations an organization must meet: laws, regulations, contracts, its own policies and the standards of conduct it has promised.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Breaking them brings fines, lost licenses, lawsuits and damaged trust. The source of a requirement decides who must be told and how serious a breach is.
how_it_works: Legal and regulatory requirements come from outside and are mandatory: statutes, regulations, license conditions and court orders.
Contractual requirements (promises to customers, suppliers, lenders, partners) and internal ones (the organization's own policies, procedures and code of conduct) bind it too.
Requirements follow activities and dates: a new market, product or contract (a loan's conditions, say) binds from day one; a law binds from its start date, not its passing.
Ethical expectations go further than law: an act can be legal and still breach the organization's values or harm stakeholders.
Management owns compliance and usually runs compliance and ethics programs; the board oversees them.
The internal audit plan must consider coverage of how effective those programs are (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan).
subtopics.example: A payments firm in Brazil sells customer spending data to advertisers. Local law does not ban the practice, but the firm's own privacy promise says data is never sold. Internal auditor Camila, reviewing data handling, identifies the sale as a breach of an internal commitment and an ethical expectation even though it is legal. Camila documents the criteria and reports it as a finding.

review: Compare the obligations register with the laws and contracts that apply
Sample obligations and trace each to an owner and a control
Inspect how new or changed rules are picked up
evidence: Register of legal, regulatory and contractual obligations with owners
Regulator correspondence and inspection results
Breach log with causes and actions taken
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to keep a current obligations register with an owner and a control for each requirement.
audit_focus.decides: Management answers for meeting each obligation; the board oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the source of the requirement first: law, contract, policy or ethical expectation. Legal is the floor, not the ceiling. Management owns compliance; the internal auditor assesses and reports. Must: the plan considers coverage of the compliance and ethics programs (Standard 9.4).

exam_traps.trap: If it is legal, it is ethical, so there is nothing to report.
exam_traps.why: Law is a minimum. Conduct can be lawful and still break the organization's code or commitments, which makes it reportable.

exam_traps.trap: Compliance only means obeying laws.
exam_traps.why: Compliance also covers regulations, contracts, policies, procedures and other requirements that bind the organization.

key_terms.definition: Meeting the binding rules that apply: law, regulation, contract and the organization's own policies.
A document stating the behavior an organization expects from its people.
Management's organized effort to know its obligations, meet them and catch breaches.

subtopics.name: The Internal Auditor's Place in the Ethics Framework
subtopics.definition: The internal auditor's role in the ethics framework is to promote an ethics-based culture, assess how well ethics and compliance are managed, and report concerns, without owning the program.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Ethics programs fail when nobody independent tests them. An internal audit function that runs the hotline or disciplines staff is doing management's work and cannot give objective assurance over it.
how_it_works: Internal auditors must respect and meet the organization's legitimate ethical expectations and encourage an ethics-based culture (Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations).
They must be able to recognize conduct that goes against those expectations.
The internal audit plan must consider how effective the compliance and ethics programs are; in each engagement, auditors should also weigh the ethics side of its risks and controls.
Concerns must be reported through the channels that policy and law set, and never held back.
Management owns the code, training, discipline and the decision on what to do about a concern. Internal audit investigates only where its mandate and skills allow.
subtopics.example: At a polytechnic in Ghana, internal auditor Kwame learns that internal audit has run the staff ethics hotline for two years 'because audit is trusted', with nothing in the charter. Kwame tells the engagement supervisor that this is a role beyond internal auditing, so internal audit cannot assess the hotline objectively. The chief audit executive reports the impairment to the board and senior management and proposes handing the hotline back to management.

review: Sample hotline cases and trace each to its closure
Compare ethics training completion records with the staff list
Interview staff on whether raising a concern feels safe
evidence: Hotline case log with dates, outcomes and escalations
Signed code of conduct acknowledgments
Ethics training attendance records
audit_focus.recommend: Get management to name a clear owner for the ethics program and report case trends to the board.
audit_focus.decides: Management runs the ethics program; the board oversees it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Musts: promote an ethics-based culture and report concerns. Should: consider ethics risks in each engagement. Running part of the program, such as a hotline, is a role beyond internal auditing: it must be discussed with the board, written into the charter with safeguards and assured by another independent party.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit should run the whistleblower hotline because it is independent.
exam_traps.why: Running it is a role beyond internal auditing, which needs the safeguards set out in 1A8.4.

exam_traps.trap: An internal auditor who finds misconduct should discipline the employee involved.
exam_traps.why: Discipline is management's decision. The auditor reports through the set channel.

key_terms.definition: The code, training, reporting channels and follow-up an organization uses to guide and check behavior.
A confidential channel for reporting suspected wrongdoing, often anonymously.

subtopics.name: Reporting Ethics and Compliance Concerns
subtopics.definition: Reporting an ethics or compliance concern means passing the internal auditor's findings to people with authority to act, by the route policy, law and the internal audit function's methodology set.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A concern sent to the wrong person can be buried, and one sent outside the proper route can break confidentiality or law.
how_it_works: Behavior that goes against the organization's ethical expectations must be reported in line with its policies and procedures (Standard 1.2).
Legal or regulatory violations must go to people or bodies with authority to act, as law, regulation and policy specify (Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior).
In practice the internal auditor tells the engagement supervisor or the chief audit executive (CAE), who follows the function's methodology.
If a member of senior management is involved, the CAE should report it to the board; if the board chair is involved, to the entire board.
A concern is reportable even when it falls outside the engagement's scope.
The auditor reports facts and evidence; those with authority decide what happens next.
subtopics.example: While testing maintenance records at a port authority in Vietnam, internal auditor Hoang learns that the chief operating officer told crane inspectors to sign off inspections that were never done. Crane safety is outside the engagement scope. Hoang keeps the evidence, does not question the chief operating officer and tells the CAE, who takes the matter to the board because a member of senior management is involved.

review: Trace a sample of reported concerns from receipt to the person who acted
Compare the route each concern took with the ethics policy
evidence: Concern log showing dates, recipients and outcomes
Ethics policy naming who receives each kind of concern
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to state in policy who receives each kind of concern and how matters about senior management reach the board.
audit_focus.decides: The board or the responsible managers choose what follows

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: report the concern through the channel that policy and law set, to someone with authority to act. Should: where senior management is involved, the CAE takes it to the board. Do not discipline, and do not stay silent because it is out of scope.

exam_traps.trap: The issue is outside the engagement scope, so the auditor may leave it.
exam_traps.why: The duty to report unethical or illegal conduct does not depend on scope.

exam_traps.trap: Raise the concern first with the manager whose conduct is in question.
exam_traps.why: It goes through the set channel to someone with authority to act; a senior management matter should reach the board.

key_terms.definition: The route that policy, law or the function's methodology sets for raising a concern.
The power to investigate, correct or sanction a violation.

topics.overview: Risk is what uncertainty can do to an objective. This topic covers how to sort a risk by the objective it threatens (strategy, operations, finances, compliance, reputation, and environmental, social and sustainability matters) and how to tell inherent risk from residual risk in a scenario.
can_do: Classify a risk in a scenario as strategic, financial, operational, compliance, reputational or sustainability-related
Explain why reputational harm often follows another risk event, and when reputational risk is still the best label
Work out inherent and residual risk from the facts of a case

subtopics.name: Risk and Its Main Categories
subtopics.definition: Risk is what uncertainty can do to an objective, for better or worse; risk categories sort risks by the kind of objective they threaten.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Sorting a risk correctly points to who owns it and what kind of control fits. Exam scenarios describe an event and ask which type of risk it is, so read for the objective that is hit.
how_it_works: Risk attaches to objectives. Start by asking which objective the event would damage or help.
Categories group risks by the objective affected. The Standards name strategic, operational, financial and compliance without defining them; each organization sets its own.
One event often touches several categories. Classify by the objective most directly affected, then note the knock-on effects.
Appetite can differ by type of risk (1C5.2). A finding's significance must weigh likelihood and impact, and should weigh tolerance and other factors that matter (Standard 14.3).
Risk is two-sided: uncertainty can help an objective as well as harm it, so opportunities belong in the picture.
Internal auditors may consider these categories when gathering information for an engagement (Standard 13.2, considerations).

types.meaning: The chosen direction or business model may be wrong, or may be overtaken by outside change.
Day-to-day work may fail or be disrupted through people, processes, systems or outside events.
Money may be lost or funding may fall short.
A law, regulation, contract or internal policy may be broken.

subtopics.example: A food exporter in Argentina signs a five-year contract priced in a foreign currency, then sees the exchange rate swing against it. In the same month a packing-line breakdown delays shipments. Internal auditor Lucía, updating the engagement risk assessment, classifies the currency exposure as financial risk and the breakdown as operational risk, and links each risk to its owner and control.

review: Compare the risk register's categories with the organization's stated objectives
Sample register entries and confirm each has a named owner
Inspect how a risk spanning several categories is recorded once
evidence: Risk register showing category, owner and rating for each risk
Risk category definitions approved by management
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to define its risk categories in writing and assign one accountable owner to every risk.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns each risk and how it is classified

subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify a risk by the objective it most directly threatens, then ask what follows from it. May: internal auditors consider the four categories the Standards name in a consideration. The Standards define none, so this sorting is a study aid.

exam_traps.trap: Risk only means something bad that might happen.
exam_traps.why: The Standards treat risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, which can be positive or negative. Opportunity is part of risk.

exam_traps.trap: Every risk fits exactly one category.
exam_traps.why: One event can threaten several objectives. Name the most direct one and note the others as consequences.

key_terms.definition: What uncertainty may do to an objective, for better or worse.
A label that groups risks by the kind of objective they affect.
How probable it is that an event happens.
The size of the consequence if the event happens.

subtopics.name: Reputational and Sustainability-Related Risk
subtopics.definition: Reputational risk is the chance that stakeholders lose trust in the organization; sustainability-related risk covers environmental, social responsibility and long-term viability matters that can affect its objectives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Boards oversee more than financial risk, and internal auditors look beyond it too.
how_it_works: Reputational damage is often an effect: it follows another event, such as a safety failure, a data breach or an ethics scandal.
So reputation is protected mostly by managing the underlying risks and responding openly to failures.
Environmental, social and sustainability risks run both ways: the world's effect on the organization, and its effect on the world, which can rebound through claims, fines or lost permits.
They turn financial through fines, lost customers, higher costs or lost funding.
Public claims about them need evidence behind them, just as financial figures do.
The chief audit executive (CAE) should ask the board what it expects on nonfinancial concerns such as sustainability and reputation (Standard 8.1 Board Interaction, considerations).
subtopics.example: A Bangladeshi garment maker passes a customer's labor audit, but a news report later shows a subcontractor using unsafe premises; orders are paused. Senior internal auditor Farah, reviewing supplier management, records a social responsibility risk in the supply chain and the reputational risk that followed it. Farah assesses the controls over subcontractor approval, where the cause sits, and reports the gap.

review: Trace a reputational incident back to the event that caused it
Compare published sustainability figures with the supporting records
Inspect how environmental and social risks enter the risk register
evidence: Source data behind published sustainability figures
Incident and complaint logs with root causes
Board papers on environmental and social matters
audit_focus.recommend: Get management to name owners for environmental and social risks and verify public statements against evidence before release.
audit_focus.decides: The board sets expectations; management owns these risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Reputational risk is a risk type in its own right: stakeholders losing trust. It often arrives through another event, so assess the controls over that event. Should: the CAE asks the board what it expects on reputation and sustainability (Standard 8.1, considerations).

exam_traps.trap: Reputational risk is best controlled by the communications team.
exam_traps.why: Communication handles the aftermath. Reputation is protected mainly by controlling the risks that cause the damage.

exam_traps.trap: Sustainability matters are outside the internal audit function's remit because they are nonfinancial.
exam_traps.why: Internal auditing covers governance, risk management and control for financial and nonfinancial objectives alike.

key_terms.definition: The possibility that trust in the organization falls among customers, regulators, staff or the public.
Exposure from the organization's effect on nature, or nature's effect on the organization.
Exposure from how the organization treats the people and communities it touches.
A threat to the organization's ability to keep operating and creating value over the long term.

subtopics.name: Inherent and Residual Risk
subtopics.definition: Inherent risk is the exposure before anything management does about it; residual risk is what is left after management's controls and other responses are in place.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The gap between the two shows what the controls are worth. Residual risk is what the organization actually carries, so it is the figure compared with risk appetite and tolerance.
how_it_works: Rate inherent risk as if no controls or other responses existed, counting outside factors (weather, market swings) as well as inside ones, even ones no manager could prevent.
Then take account of what management has in place: controls, insurance, contracts, contingency plans.
What remains is residual risk. It is rarely zero.
Compare residual risk with risk appetite and tolerance. Above them, more action or a decision at the right level is needed.

In an engagement, the internal auditor evaluates existing controls for design and effectiveness, then determines residual risk to judge a finding's significance (Standard 14.3 Evaluation of Findings, considerations).
High inherent risk held down by controls means heavy reliance on those controls, which is a reason to test them.

rows.label: Inherent risk
cells: Before management's actions
Seeing raw exposure and where controls matter most

rows.label: Residual risk
cells: After management's actions
Comparing with risk appetite and tolerance

subtopics.example: A cold-storage company in Norway stores vaccines. Power failure is rated high on likelihood and impact before controls. Management has backup generators, temperature alarms and insurance. Internal auditor Ingrid tests the generators and finds that one failed to start in two tests. Ingrid concludes that residual risk is higher than management's register shows, because a key control is not working, and reports the gap for management to act on.

review: Reperform the residual rating using only controls that passed testing
Trace risks rated above tolerance to a recorded decision
Inspect whether inherent ratings were set before counting controls
evidence: Test results for each control the rating relies on
Risk register showing both ratings and the controls between them
audit_focus.recommend: Have risk owners base residual ratings on tested controls and revisit a rating whenever a control fails.
audit_focus.decides: Management accepts residual risk within appetite or takes more action

subtopics.isaca_rule: Inherent is before management's actions; residual is after what management has done, not after what the auditor recommends. Residual risk is compared with appetite and tolerance. Must: judge a finding's significance by likelihood and impact (Standard 14.3).

exam_traps.trap: Residual risk is what remains after the auditor's recommendations are carried out.
exam_traps.why: It is the risk left after the management actions in place now. Recommendations not yet implemented change nothing.

exam_traps.trap: Count the existing controls when rating inherent risk.
exam_traps.why: Inherent risk ignores controls. Counting them hides how much the organization depends on those controls.

key_terms.definition: The exposure an activity carries before counting anything management does about it.
The exposure still left once management's controls and other responses are in place.

topics.overview: Risk management is management's continuing process for dealing with uncertainty, overseen by the board. This topic covers what it is, how risk appetite differs from risk tolerance, the steps of the cycle and what makes each one sound, and how to judge whether a risk response is a good one.
can_do: Explain what risk management is for and who owns it
Tell risk appetite from risk tolerance in a scenario
Place an activity in the risk management cycle and judge whether that step is sound
Judge whether a risk response fits the risk and the organization's appetite

subtopics.name: What Risk Management Is
subtopics.definition: Risk management is the ongoing process of finding, sizing up and dealing with events that could affect objectives, so the organization has reasonable assurance of reaching them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without it, risks are handled by whoever notices them. With it, the board and management can take risk on purpose, in line with strategy, and are caught out less often.
how_it_works: Management manages risk and runs the process, overseen by the board. Internal audit's risk assessment for its own plan is no substitute (The IIA's 2026 ERM statement).
Risks are identified against agreed objectives, since a risk is uncertainty's effect on them; the work ties to strategy and performance.
Enterprise risk management is the coordinated, organization-wide version: one view of risk across functions for the board and senior management.
It is continuous: a yearly register update is a record, not risk management.
It gives reasonable assurance, not certainty: some risk events will still happen.
subtopics.example: A Nepali savings cooperative's compliance officer updates its risk register each December for the regulator; branch managers have never seen it. On an advisory engagement (advice, not assurance) for the chief executive officer, internal auditor Priya points out that the register is a record, not risk management, which would have branch managers acting on risks all year. Priya sets out options and leaves the choice to management.

review: Compare risk register update dates with dates of major business changes
Trace one top risk from identification to action and reporting
Interview line managers about the risks they handle each day
evidence: Risk committee minutes showing decisions taken on risks
Risk management policy naming roles and reporting frequency
audit_focus.recommend: Get senior management to build risk identification and review into planning and performance routines, not a yearly register update.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides how risk work is organized; the board oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Risk management is management's process, overseen by the board, aimed at objectives and giving reasonable assurance. The goal is risk-taking in line with appetite, never removing all risk. Must: the chief audit executive understands how significant risks are found and assessed (Standard 9.1).

exam_traps.trap: The goal of risk management is to eliminate risk.
exam_traps.why: Pursuing objectives means taking risk. The aim is risk-taking in line with appetite and tolerance, not the least risk possible.

exam_traps.trap: Enterprise risk management is the risk department.
exam_traps.why: It is an organization-wide approach carried out by management at all levels, not a department.

key_terms.definition: Management's continuing process for spotting, weighing and dealing with events that bear on objectives.
Risk management done as one joined-up effort across the whole organization, giving leaders a single view of threats and opportunities.
Well-founded confidence, never certainty, that risk management and control give about meeting objectives.
A list of identified risks with their ratings, owners and responses.

subtopics.name: Risk Appetite and Risk Tolerance
subtopics.definition: Risk appetite is how much risk, and of what kinds, an organization chooses to take in pursuing its strategy; risk tolerance is the acceptable swing in results around an objective.
subtopics.why_it_matters: They are the yardsticks for risk decisions. The internal auditor's test for 'too much risk' is the organization's appetite or tolerance, never the auditor's own comfort.
how_it_works: Risk appetite: both of The IIA's 2026 Statements of Position say the board establishes it; management proposes it and works inside it.
Risk tolerance: the enterprise risk management Statement says the board establishes it too; the Standards' glossary names nobody.
Appetite is broad and strategic; tolerance is narrow and measurable, such as on-time delivery of 95 percent with 93 to 97 percent acceptable.
Appetite works both ways: the 2026 ERM statement wants it built into decisions, so choices taking far less risk than the strategy needs can be a weakness too.
When planning an engagement, internal auditors gather information on risk tolerance, if set (Standard 13.2).
Residual risk is compared with both. Risk accepted above either is the trigger in Standard 11.5 Communicating the Acceptance of Risks.

rows.label: Risk appetite
cells: The whole organization; established by the board
'We accept very little risk to customer safety.'

rows.label: Risk tolerance
cells: One objective or measure. The enterprise risk management Statement of Position says the board establishes it; the Three Lines Statement and the Standards' glossary name nobody; Standard 8.1 mentions the board's risk tolerance
'System uptime of 99.5 percent, never below 99.'

subtopics.example: An Emirati air cargo carrier's board states a 'very low appetite for safety risk'; its maintenance target is zero overdue inspections, with up to two tolerated for five days. Internal auditor Noor finds eleven inspections overdue for a month, accepted by the maintenance manager. Noor reports the accepted risk as outside tolerance and informs the chief audit executive (CAE).

review: Confirm the board approved the current risk appetite statement
Compare operating limits with the appetite they are meant to reflect
Sample breaches of limits and trace how each was escalated
evidence: Minutes recording approval of the appetite document
Limit reports with breaches flagged
Sign-off records showing who accepted each breach
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management set out measurable tolerances for each key objective, agree them at the right level and report breaches promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The board establishes appetite; one 2026 Statement of Position gives it tolerance too

subtopics.isaca_rule: Appetite: how much risk, of what kinds, the organization will take; the board establishes it. Tolerance: the acceptable variation around an objective. The internal audit function measures against both and sets neither. Must: the CAE raises risk accepted above either (Standard 11.5).

exam_traps.trap: Risk tolerance is the total amount of risk the board is willing to take.
exam_traps.why: That describes appetite. Tolerance is the acceptable variation in performance around one objective.

exam_traps.trap: Where no appetite is defined, internal audit should set one so that risks can be assessed.
exam_traps.why: Establishing appetite is the board's role. Internal audit reports the gap and can advise on the process.

key_terms.definition: How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.

subtopics.name: The Risk Management Cycle
subtopics.definition: The risk management cycle is the repeating sequence of identifying risks, assessing them, managing them, monitoring what changes and reporting to those who oversee.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A weakness at any step undermines the rest: a risk never identified is never managed, and a risk never reported cannot be overseen.
how_it_works: Identify means finding threats and opportunities linked to objectives. It is sound when it is complete, uses one risk language and follows strategy.
Assess means rating likelihood and impact and ranking the risks. It is sound when the method is consistent and assumptions are challenged.
Manage means choosing and carrying out responses and controls. It is sound when responses bring risk within appetite and have owners.
Monitor means watching for changes in risks and whether responses still work. It is sound when it is timely and uses indicators.
Report means telling senior management and the board. It is sound when significant risks are escalated clearly and promptly.

The cycle repeats and feeds back. The Standards' glossary uses four verbs (identify, assess, manage, control); The IIA's 2026 enterprise risk management statement lists identify, assess, manage, monitor, report.
subtopics.example: A credit union in Hawaii runs a risk workshop each January and rates forty risks. Nothing is revisited until the next January. Internal auditor Leilani, assessing the risk management process, finds that an online lending product launched in June never entered the register. Leilani concludes that identification and monitoring are weak, since the cycle ran once instead of continuously, and reports this with the lending product as evidence.

review: Trace a recent business change into the risk identification records
Reperform a sample of risk ratings using the stated method
Compare the risks reported to the board with the full register
evidence: Key risk indicator reports with thresholds and trends
Risk rating method with its scales
Board risk reports for the past year
audit_focus.recommend: Have management set triggers that send new products, projects and incidents into risk identification and review.
audit_focus.decides: Management runs the cycle; the board oversees the results

subtopics.isaca_rule: Identify, assess, manage, monitor, report, then repeat. Management carries out each step; the internal audit function assesses each step and may advise. The five steps come from The IIA's 2026 statement, not from a requirement of the Standards.

exam_traps.trap: Monitoring risks is internal audit's step in the cycle.
exam_traps.why: Management monitors its own risks and responses. Internal audit assesses whether that monitoring works, and tracks only the action plans that come from its own engagements.

exam_traps.trap: Once responses are in place, the process is complete.
exam_traps.why: Risks and responses change. Monitoring and reporting keep the picture current and feed the next round.

key_terms.definition: Scoring a risk, usually by likelihood and impact, so risks can be ranked.
A measure that gives early warning that a risk is growing.

subtopics.name: Risk Responses and How to Judge Them
subtopics.definition: A risk response is what management chooses to do about a risk, such as accepting it, reducing it, sharing it with another party or avoiding it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The response decides the residual risk. Internal auditors are asked whether a response is adequate: whether it fits the risk and brings it within appetite at a sensible cost.
how_it_works: Management selects the response for each significant risk and names an owner; responses can be combined.
Accepting is legitimate within appetite and tolerance and should be recorded; sharing moves part of the loss, never the accountability.
Judge a response by whether residual risk now falls within appetite and tolerance, at a cost in proportion to the risk.
The internal audit function gives assurance on whether responses are adequate. It must not select, implement or own them.
Acceptance above appetite or tolerance: the CAE should first take it up with the responsible manager and agree an updated plan (Standard 11.5, considerations).
If that fails, the CAE must raise it with senior management, then the board if unresolved; resolving is not the CAE's job. Slipping plans can be acceptance (Standard 15.2).

types.meaning: Take no further action and bear the risk knowingly.
Add or strengthen controls to lower likelihood, impact or both.
Pass part of the loss to another party, for example by insurance or contract.
Stop, or never start, the activity that creates the risk.

subtopics.example: A South African telecom company stores customer records with a cloud provider and buys cyber insurance. The risk register shows data-breach risk as 'transferred: no residual risk'. Internal auditor Thabo notes that the policy excludes regulatory fines and that the firm stays accountable to customers and the regulator. Thabo reports that the response shares only part of the loss and that management should re-rate the residual risk against appetite.

review: Compare each response with the risk's rating and the stated appetite
Inspect insurance and contract terms for exclusions and caps
Sample accepted risks and confirm who signed each acceptance
evidence: Risk acceptance records with approver, reason and date
Insurance schedules and contract clauses the response relies on
Cost and benefit workings behind major responses
audit_focus.recommend: Ask risk owners to record the chosen response, its cost and the residual risk, and to obtain approval at the right level.
audit_focus.decides: Risk owners choose; the board has the last word above appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: A good response fits the risk, brings residual risk within appetite and tolerance at a proportionate cost, and has an owner. Management chooses it, never the auditor. Must: the CAE escalates acceptance above appetite or tolerance (Standard 11.5).

exam_traps.trap: Insurance removes the risk.
exam_traps.why: Insurance shares the financial loss up to its limits. The event can still happen; accountability and uncovered losses remain.

exam_traps.trap: Any risk that management chose to accept is an audit finding.
exam_traps.why: Acceptance within appetite is a legitimate response; Standard 11.5 escalation starts only above appetite or tolerance. Far less risk than the strategy needs can still be a weakness.

key_terms.definition: What management chooses to do about a risk.
A knowing decision to bear a risk without further action.

topics.overview: This topic looks at risk management as a whole: how an internal auditor judges whether it is well set up and working, where internal audit's own involvement must stop, and why organizations build their risk management on a recognized framework.
can_do: Describe what internal audit looks at when it assesses risk management
Separate the risk management work internal audit may do from the decisions it must leave to management
Explain why an organization adopts a risk management framework and what it gains

subtopics.name: Assessing How Risk Management Is Designed and Works
subtopics.definition: Assessing risk management means judging whether the organization's risk processes are set up sensibly for its size and strategy, and whether they work in practice as intended.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board relies on these processes to know its risks. If they are weak, risk reports cannot be trusted, and the internal audit function cannot lean on management's risk information when planning its own work.
how_it_works: Design asks whether roles are clear, risk appetite is established, one method and language are used and the whole organization is covered.
Operation asks whether risks are identified and rated consistently, significant risks are escalated and responses match what the board expects.
Use and culture ask whether risk information drives decisions, and whether incentives bias it: ratings set by people paid more for favorable ones are not reliable evidence.
In combined reporting the CAE must still flag first- or second-line information that is wrong, partial or unreliable (The IIA's 2026 ERM statement, a guide).

Should (Standard 9.4, considerations): rely on management's risk information only after concluding the process is effective, reevaluate that reliance, and independently validate key risks without taking over management's ratings.
Weak or young processes: internal audit identifies more risks itself and may lean toward advice; mature ones, toward assurance.
subtopics.example: At a ceramics manufacturer in Türkiye, internal auditor Elif drafts next year's engagement list straight from management's risk register. Elif then checks how it is made: only two of nine plants contribute, and ratings have not changed in three years. The process cannot yet be relied on, so the chief audit executive (CAE) does more of internal audit's own risk identification. Even a sound register would only feed the CAE's documented assessment, never replace it.

review: Compare who contributes to the risk register with the organization chart
Trace significant risks from business units through to board reports
Sample major decisions and inspect the risk information used
evidence: Risk management policy with roles and escalation thresholds
Board risk reports set beside the underlying register
Decision papers showing risk analysis before approval
audit_focus.recommend: Get senior management to extend risk identification to all units and set clear escalation thresholds for significant risks.
audit_focus.decides: The board judges whether risk oversight meets its needs

subtopics.isaca_rule: Assess the process before trusting its output. Must: the plan rests on the CAE's own documented risk assessment (Standard 9.4). Should: rely on management's risk information only after concluding that its risk management processes are effective.

exam_traps.trap: Management keeps a detailed risk register, so internal audit can base its plan on it.
exam_traps.why: A register is an output. Internal audit should first conclude that the process producing it is effective.

key_terms.definition: How developed and embedded an organization's risk management is.
Using another party's work or information instead of repeating it, after judging it trustworthy.

subtopics.name: Internal Audit's Boundaries in Risk Management
subtopics.definition: The internal audit function's boundary in risk management is the line between assuring and advising on the process, which it may do, and making risk decisions, which belongs to management.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Internal auditors who know risk well are often asked to run risk management. Each step over the line weakens the independent assurance the board receives.
how_it_works: Internal audit may give assurance on any step of the cycle, advise on methods, facilitate workshops and training, challenge assumptions and share good practice.
For its own planning, it assesses risks to prioritize the internal audit plan and watches for emerging risks.
It must not prioritize, select, implement or own risk responses, own management's follow-up, or be accountable for risk decisions.
Advisory work on risk management is scoped and documented as advisory and leaves responsibility with management.
If the chief audit executive takes on risk management duties, the safeguards in 1A8.4 apply (Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence).
Who may give later assurance after such work is covered in 1B2.4; merely advising is no automatic bar.

rows.label: Identify
cells: Advise on risk language without setting management's approach; assure completeness
Determine or own risk responses

rows.label: Assess
cells: Advise on rating methods without running the ongoing assessment; assure the ratings
Prioritize risk responses

rows.label: Manage
cells: Advise on policies and controls; assure responses
Select, implement or own responses

rows.label: Monitor
cells: Advise on indicators; assure management's monitoring
Own management's follow-up

rows.label: Report
cells: Advise on clarity; assure escalation
Own reporting to outside parties

subtopics.example: At a power utility in Zambia, internal auditor Zanele assesses the risk management process. Zanele traces three new projects into the risk register, reperforms a sample of ratings and checks that risks above the escalation threshold reached the board. Two had not. Asked by the chief executive officer to pick which risks get funding, Zanele declines and reports the gaps.

review: Inspect the charter for any risk management duty held by internal audit
Compare advisory files on risk management with the decisions management recorded as its own
evidence: Terms of advisory engagements on risk management, with their stated limits
Register showing the named owner of every risk response
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management name an owner outside internal audit for the risk register and for each risk response.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides risk responses; the board oversees them

subtopics.isaca_rule: Assure and advise on risk management; never decide. An option that has internal audit choosing, prioritizing, implementing or owning a risk response is wrong. Source: The IIA's 2026 enterprise risk management statement and Standards 2.2 and 7.1. Limits and safeguards: 1A8.3, 1A8.4.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit assures only the risk register, the output of the process.
exam_traps.why: Assurance covers every step of the cycle: how risks are identified, rated, responded to, monitored and reported, not only the list that results.

exam_traps.trap: With safeguards in place, internal audit can assure risk management work it performed itself.
exam_traps.why: Disclosure and documentation do not remove self-review bias. Assurance over work internal audit performed or supervised must come from another independent party.

key_terms.definition: Guiding a discussion or workshop so that management reaches its own conclusions.
Losing a critical eye when assessing work one designed, decided or performed oneself.

subtopics.name: Why Organizations Use a Risk Management Framework
subtopics.definition: A risk management framework is a published set of principles and components that an organization adapts to build, run and judge its own risk management.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a shared reference, each unit manages risk its own way and the board cannot add up what it is told.
how_it_works: Purpose: structure and a common language, so risk is managed the same way across the organization and tied to strategy.
Benefits: fewer unwelcome shocks, steadier performance, better use of resources, more opportunities seen, greater resilience.
One example is COSO's Enterprise Risk Management framework (2017), which ties risk to strategy and performance through five components, the first being governance and culture.
Frameworks rest on broad principles, so a small organization applies them more simply than a large one.
For internal auditors, a framework the organization has adopted supplies evaluation criteria.
A framework is a guide, not a guarantee. The enterprise approach links each unit's risk work into one view and never replaces it (The IIA's 2026 ERM statement).
subtopics.example: A Colombian farm cooperative has six regions that each rate risk on a different scale, so the board's risk report cannot be added up. Asked by the board for advice, the chief audit executive (CAE), Andrés, explains that a recognized framework would give one language, one rating method and a checklist of components. Andrés leaves the choice of framework and its rollout to management and the board.

review: Confirm which risk framework management adopted and how it was tailored
Compare the framework's components with what exists in practice
Inspect whether every unit uses the same rating scales
evidence: Adoption paper approved by the board or risk committee
Gap assessment against the framework's components
Unit risk reports showing the scales in use
audit_focus.recommend: Ask senior management to adopt one risk framework for all units, tailor it to size and track gaps to closure.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management choose and adopt the framework

subtopics.isaca_rule: A risk management framework is there for consistency, completeness and a common language linked to strategy. Do not treat adoption as proof that risks are well managed. Should: the CAE understands the recognized ones (Standard 9.1, considerations).

exam_traps.trap: We adopted a recognized framework, so our risk management is effective.
exam_traps.why: A framework describes what good looks like. Effectiveness depends on how it is applied, which still has to be assessed.

exam_traps.trap: Risk management frameworks suit only large listed companies.
exam_traps.why: They scale: they are meant for organizations of any size or sector.

key_terms.definition: A reference set of principles and components for building and judging risk management.
The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations (COSO) of the Treadway Commission, backed by five professional bodies including The IIA; it publishes control, risk and fraud guidance.
Shared terms and rating scales, so risks from different units can be compared.

topics.topic_name: Internal control concepts and control types
topics.overview: Controls are what management, the board or other parties do to keep risks in check so objectives can be met. This topic covers what controls are for, how to tell preventive, detective, corrective and directive controls apart, and how to suggest a control that fits the risk without doing management's job.
can_do: Explain what a control is for by linking it to a risk and an objective
Classify a control as preventive, detective, corrective or directive from what it does and when it acts
Choose a control recommendation that fits the root cause, the size of the risk and its cost

subtopics.name: The Purpose of Internal Control
subtopics.definition: A control is anything management, the board or others do to keep a risk in check and so improve the odds of reaching an objective.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls are how risk responses become real. They exist to serve objectives, so a control with no risk behind it is waste, and a significant risk with no control is a gap.
how_it_works: Controls serve objectives such as effective and efficient operations, reliable information, safeguarded assets and compliance.
Control processes are the routines an organization designs and runs to keep risks within tolerance.
Management designs, runs and owns most controls; the board's acts, such as approving large contracts, and other parties' checks can be controls too.
Internal control gives reasonable assurance, not a guarantee, that objectives will be met.
Controls apply to financial and nonfinancial objectives alike, such as safety, service quality or data protection.
The internal audit function assesses whether control processes are adequate and effective; it does not operate them.
subtopics.example: A Malaysian clinic has every prescription checked by a second pharmacist. A manager complains it slows the queue and asks what it is for. Internal auditor Aisyah, reviewing dispensing, links the control to its objective, patient safety, and to the risk it manages, a wrong dose reaching a patient. Aisyah confirms the check works and reports that nothing similar covers dispensing at night.

review: Trace each key control to the risk and objective it serves
Confirm every significant risk has at least one control
Observe the control being performed, not only its description
evidence: Traces the control leaves when performed, such as sign-offs
Risk and control records naming the owner of each control
Procedure documents for the key controls
audit_focus.recommend: Have process owners link every control to a risk and fix or remove those that serve none.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns controls and judges how much control is enough

subtopics.isaca_rule: Objective first, then risk, then control. Management owns and runs most controls, but the board's acts and other parties' checks, such as a contractor's, count too. The internal auditor assesses them. Controls give reasonable assurance, never absolute assurance. Must: assurance conclusions state whether control processes are effective (Standard 14.5).

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditor ensures that controls work.
exam_traps.why: Management is responsible for controls working. The internal auditor gives assurance by assessing them and reporting.

exam_traps.trap: Internal control is about financial reporting.
exam_traps.why: Controls serve operations, reporting of all kinds, safeguarding of assets and compliance, financial and nonfinancial.

key_terms.definition: Something management, the board or others do to keep a risk in check and make an objective more reachable.
The rules, routines and checks that hold risks inside the organization's risk tolerance.
What a control is meant to achieve, stated as the risk it should keep in check.
A control the organization depends on most to manage a significant risk.

subtopics.name: Preventive, Detective, Corrective and Directive Controls
subtopics.definition: Control types describe what a control does and when it acts: preventive controls stop a problem before it happens, detective controls find it afterward, and corrective controls put it right.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Naming the type tells you what a control can and cannot do. A detective control never stops the first error, so relying on it alone for a high-impact risk leaves a gap.
how_it_works: Ask what the control does and when. One that stops the event beforehand is preventive; one that reveals it afterward is detective; one that repairs the damage is corrective.
Directive controls tell people what should happen, through policies, training and instructions. The Standards list four types (Standard 13.2, considerations) and define none of them.
Preventive and detective are the firm pair: COSO's control framework names them too. Corrective and directive are described here by the plain meaning of the words.
A detective control needs follow-up to be worth anything: an exception report that nobody reviews controls nothing.
Sound design mixes the types, so that what prevention misses, detection catches and correction repairs.

types.meaning: Acts before the event to stop it. Example: an approval required before a payment is released.
Acts after the event to reveal it. Example: a bank reconciliation or an exception report.
Plain meaning: acts after detection to repair the damage. Example: restoring lost data from a backup.
Plain meaning: tells people what is expected. Example: a written policy or instruction.

subtopics.example: At a transit operator in Chile, duplicate supplier payments are found each month by a reconciliation and then recovered from suppliers. Management calls the reconciliation 'our preventive control'. Internal auditor Ignacio, reviewing payables, points out that it is detective, since the money has already left, and that the recovery step is corrective. Ignacio recommends that management consider a preventive control, such as a system block on repeated invoice numbers.

review: Classify each key control by when it acts on the risk
Sample exceptions from a detective control and trace the follow-up
Compare the mix of control types with each risk's impact
evidence: System settings showing which checks block a transaction
Exception reports with proof of review and resolution
Control descriptions stating the timing of each control
audit_focus.recommend: Get process owners to add preventive controls where one event would be costly and to assign follow-up for every detective control.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the mix of control types for each risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify by what the control does: stops the event (preventive), reveals it afterward (detective), repairs it (corrective) or tells people what is expected (directive). A reconciliation or a review is detective, however often it runs. The four types sit in a consideration; none is a must.

exam_traps.trap: A daily reconciliation is preventive because it runs so often.
exam_traps.why: Frequency does not change the type. A reconciliation finds differences after transactions have happened, so it is detective.

exam_traps.trap: Detective controls are weaker and should always be replaced by preventive ones.
exam_traps.why: Each type has a job. Prevention can be costly or impractical, and good design combines the types.

key_terms.definition: A report that lists items falling outside set rules, for someone to review.
Comparing two records that should agree and following up every difference.

subtopics.name: Recommending Controls That Fit the Risk
subtopics.definition: A fitting control recommendation is one that addresses the root cause of a finding, brings the risk to an acceptable level and costs less than the harm it prevents.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A recommendation that ignores cause or cost gets rejected or, worse, implemented without fixing anything. Here the internal audit function is most tempted to do management's job.
how_it_works: Start from the root cause, not the symptom: a control aimed at a symptom lets the problem return.
Match the control to the risk: weigh cost against benefit and bring the risk within tolerance.
Internal auditors decide whether to develop recommendations, request management's action plan, or agree actions jointly with management (Standard 14.4).
Recommendations must be discussed with the management of the activity under review.
Afterward, internal auditors confirm the agreed action was implemented; they do not build or run the control.
An alternative plan agreed to be satisfactory or better than the original should be tracked (Standard 15.2, considerations); a disagreement must follow the established methodology (Standard 14.4).
subtopics.example: At a textile mill in Pakistan, internal auditor Ravi finds that returned fabric is sometimes credited twice. The cause: credit notes are raised from emailed requests, with no link to goods received back. Ravi discusses two options with the finance manager: a system rule requiring a goods-returned number for each credit note, or a weekly check of credits against the returns log. The finance manager chooses, and Ravi records the agreed action plan.

review: Trace each recommendation back to the finding's root cause
Compare what each option would cost with the loss it prevents
Confirm the action plan names an owner and a date
evidence: Workpaper tracing the finding to its underlying cause
Management's action plan with owners and target dates
Cost and benefit notes for the options considered
audit_focus.recommend: Have the process owner adopt the option that deals with why the gap arose, scaled to the exposure.
audit_focus.decides: The management of the activity picks the fix and carries it out

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must (Standard 14.4): discuss recommendations with the management of the activity. Should: weigh cost against benefit and risk tolerance. Aim at the root cause; management decides and implements. More control is not always better control.

exam_traps.trap: The safest recommendation is always to add another control.
exam_traps.why: Controls cost money and time. A recommendation should be in proportion to the risk and may be to remove a control.

exam_traps.trap: A compensating control solves the underlying problem.
exam_traps.why: It lowers the remaining risk, which counts when the finding is rated, while the preferred control is missing. The root cause is still there and should be noted.

key_terms.definition: The deeper reason a gap exists, as opposed to its visible symptom.
A common-usage term for an alternative control that reduces risk when the preferred control is not practical.

topics.overview: A control can fail because it was badly designed, because it is not carried out, or because it costs more than it is worth. This topic covers how design and operation are reviewed for financial and nonfinancial controls, why no control gives absolute assurance, and what an internal control framework is for.
can_do: Tell a design weakness from an operating failure
Separate effective from efficient, and reasonable from absolute assurance
Recognize what an internal control framework is for and what it does not prove

subtopics.name: Control Design and Operating Effectiveness
subtopics.definition: Control design is whether a control, if performed as intended, would manage its risk; operating effectiveness is whether it is in fact performed that way, consistently.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A badly designed control cannot work however faithfully people follow it, so testing only whether it was performed can give false comfort.
how_it_works: The design question is whether the control addresses the risk, acts at the right point and has a capable performer with the information needed.
Design may be judged first, during planning, because it shows which key controls are worth testing (Standards 13.2 and 13.6, considerations).
Where the design is inadequate, that gap is already a potential finding; testing whether the control was performed adds little, though more analysis may be needed to size the effect.
