The operation question is whether, over the period, the control was done every time, by the right person, with exceptions followed up.
A design failure is fixed by changing the control; an operating failure by training, supervision or resources.
The same two questions apply to financial and nonfinancial controls.

rows.label: Design
cells: Would it manage the risk if done as written?
Walk-through, procedure, system settings

rows.label: Operation
cells: Was it done as written, every time?
Samples, observation, repeating the control

subtopics.example: At a wholesaler in Jordan, internal auditor Rania samples sixty credit-limit increases and finds a supervisor's approval on every one. The engagement supervisor asks what the approver sees. Rania walks the process and learns that supervisors approve on screen without the customer's payment history. Rania changes the conclusion: the control is performed but inadequately designed, and reports the design gap.

review: Walk one transaction through the control before sampling any
Reperform the control on a sample drawn across the whole period
Inspect the screens and data available to whoever approves
evidence: Reperformance results for the sampled items
Walk-through notes showing each step and who performs it
Records of exceptions and how each was resolved
audit_focus.recommend: Ask process owners to redesign controls that cannot manage their risk before retraining staff to follow them.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the control and decides how to fix it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Two questions: would it work if done (design), and is it done (operation)? May: judge design first, during planning, the order the considerations describe. A design gap is a potential finding even if performed, sized with other working controls counted; testing its performance gives little assurance.

exam_traps.trap: The control was performed on every sampled item, so it is effective.
exam_traps.why: Perfect operation of a control that does not address the risk manages nothing.

exam_traps.trap: A design weakness can be fixed by reminding staff to follow the procedure.
exam_traps.why: Staff may already follow it exactly. The control itself has to change.

key_terms.definition: Whether a control, performed as written, would keep its risk at an acceptable level.
Whether a control actually works as designed, consistently, over the period.
Following one transaction from start to finish to see how the process really works.

subtopics.name: Effectiveness, Efficiency and the Limits of Control
subtopics.definition: An effective control achieves its purpose of managing the risk; an efficient control does so with no more cost, time or friction than the risk deserves.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Organizations can be over-controlled as well as under-controlled. Layers of slow, duplicated checks cost money and push people to work around them, and still no control is absolute.
how_it_works: Effective and efficient are separate tests: a control can stop every error and still cost far more than the errors would.
Efficiency looks at cost, time and duplication. Redundant or ineffective controls are candidates for removal.
Engagement findings can include chances to improve efficiency, not only control gaps.
No control system gives absolute assurance: judgment can be wrong, people make mistakes, managers can override controls and people can collude.
Events outside the organization's control can also defeat sound controls.
The same tests apply to nonfinancial objectives such as safety, quality, service and data protection.
subtopics.example: A regional museum in Spain requires five sign-offs on every purchase under 200 euros. Orders take three weeks, so staff now buy small items with their own money and claim them as expenses, and losses on small purchases are tiny. Internal auditor Marta, reviewing purchasing, reports that the control is inefficient for the risk and, because purchases now go around it, not effective either. Marta discusses a lighter control with management, which sets the new limits.

review: Compare the cost and delay of a control with the loss it prevents
Inspect for controls that duplicate each other on one risk
Observe whether staff work around slow controls
evidence: Processing-time and cost data for the controlled step
Loss and error data for the risk the control addresses
Control inventory showing overlaps on the same risk
audit_focus.recommend: Get process owners to scale each control to its risk and remove duplicates that add cost without reducing risk.
audit_focus.decides: Management, overseen by the board, judges how much control is enough

subtopics.isaca_rule: Effective means the risk is managed; efficient means at a proportionate cost. Neither means absolute assurance: judgment, error, override, collusion and outside events limit every control system. These limits come from COSO's framework, as background, not from a requirement of the Standards.

exam_traps.trap: A control that works is by definition efficient.
exam_traps.why: Effectiveness is about managing the risk; efficiency is about the cost of doing so. A working control can still be wasteful.

exam_traps.trap: Strong controls guarantee that objectives will be met.
exam_traps.why: Controls give reasonable assurance only. Human error, poor judgment, override, collusion and outside events remain.

key_terms.definition: The degree to which a control achieves what it is meant to achieve.
Achieving the result with a proportionate use of time, money and effort.
Two or more people working together to get around a control.
Built-in reasons no control system is perfect, such as error, poor judgment and override.

subtopics.name: Why Organizations Use an Internal Control Framework
subtopics.definition: An internal control framework is a published model of what a complete system of internal control contains, used to design controls and to judge whether the system works.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It turns 'do we have good controls?' into a question that can be answered the same way each time. Management, auditors and regulators can all work from one definition and one set of criteria.
how_it_works: The purpose is a shared definition of internal control and a structured way to design, run and assess it.
The benefits are consistent assessments, fewer gaps and duplicates, and clearer accountability.
One example is COSO's Internal Control framework (2013), with five components from the control environment to monitoring.
It covers operations, reporting and compliance objectives, so it reaches well beyond financial reporting.
It rests on principles applied with judgment and suits any size or type of organization; smaller ones apply it less formally.
Must (Standard 13.4): apply adequate criteria set by the board and senior management, or else identify criteria by discussion with them. A recognized framework is one example (considerations).
subtopics.example: A local council in Australia lets each department describe its controls in its own format, so the audit committee cannot tell whether controls overall are sound. The chief audit executive (CAE), Jarrah, is asked for advice. Jarrah explains that a recognized internal control framework would give every department the same components to report against and give the internal audit function consistent criteria. Jarrah leaves the adoption decision to senior management and the audit committee.

review: Confirm which control framework management uses as its reference
Compare each unit's self-assessment with the reference model's parts
Inspect whether deficiencies are reported in one consistent format
evidence: Completed self-assessment workbooks for each unit
Policy naming the adopted control framework
Deficiency reports sent to the audit committee
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management choose a single reference model and require each unit to assess itself on it identically.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management adopts the framework; the board oversees its use

subtopics.isaca_rule: An internal control framework gives a common definition, a complete structure and criteria for assessment. It is guidance applied with judgment, not a law and not a guarantee. Should: the CAE is familiar with recognized control frameworks (Standard 9.1, considerations).

exam_traps.trap: A control framework is a legal requirement that every organization must follow.
exam_traps.why: A framework is guidance. It binds only where a law, regulator or contract requires it, or the organization adopts it as policy.

exam_traps.trap: Control frameworks deal only with financial controls.
exam_traps.why: They cover operations, all kinds of reporting and compliance, so nonfinancial controls are included.

key_terms.definition: A reference model of the parts a sound system of internal control should have.
The building blocks a framework says must all be present and working together.

key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Engagement: One piece of internal audit work with its own objectives and scope.
key_terminologies.Assurance: A statement, resting on an objective assessment against criteria, that raises confidence in a process.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Governance: The board's structures and processes for informing, directing, managing and monitoring what the organization does.
key_terminologies.Board: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
key_terminologies.Three Lines Model: The IIA's model of who owns risk, who supports and challenges, and who gives independent assurance.
key_terminologies.Organizational culture: How people in an organization actually behave and work together, and what drives that behavior.
key_terminologies.Control environment: The standards, processes and structures that all other controls rest on.
key_terminologies.Tone at the top: The example about integrity and control set by the board and senior management.
key_terminologies.Compliance: Meeting the binding rules that apply: law, regulation, contract and the organization's own policies.
key_terminologies.Risk: What uncertainty may do to an objective, for better or worse.
key_terminologies.Inherent risk: The exposure an activity carries before counting anything management does about it.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The exposure still left once management's controls and other responses are in place.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.
key_terminologies.Risk management: Management's continuing process for spotting, weighing and dealing with events that bear on objectives.
key_terminologies.Risk response: What management chooses to do about a risk.
key_terminologies.Control: Something management, the board or others do to keep a risk in check and make an objective more reachable.
key_terminologies.Preventive control: A control that acts before an event to stop it from happening.
key_terminologies.Detective control: A control that acts after an event to reveal that it happened.
key_terminologies.Corrective control: In plain terms, a control that repairs the damage once a problem has been found.
key_terminologies.Directive control: In plain terms, a control that tells people what is expected, such as a written policy.
key_terminologies.Design adequacy: Whether a control, performed as written, would keep its risk at an acceptable level.
key_terminologies.Operating effectiveness: Whether a control actually works as designed, consistently, over the period.
key_terminologies.Reasonable assurance: Well-founded confidence, never certainty, that risk management and control give about meeting objectives.
key_terminologies.COSO: The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations (COSO) of the Treadway Commission, backed by five professional bodies including The IIA; it publishes control, risk and fraud guidance.
